This study presents a dynamic model designed to analyze count time series data with varying characteristics such as covariates, varying variance, and irregular intervals. A mixed model with non-linear time-varying components forms the basis of our approach, specifically a predictor-variance model that accounts for fluctuating variance and a non-linear model that incorporates exogenous variables. By extending the non-linear method with an autocorrelation component that varies over time, we derive a time-series model with both varying variance and exogenous influences. Additionally, we develop an efficient algorithm based on EM to estimate the model's parameters and a statistical test to determine the significance of external variables. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the performance of our approach and a dataset from the New York City fire department is analyzed to demonstrate its practical application.

While optical photometry is commonly used to monitor the light curves of distant stars, its potential for analyzing atmospheric conditions near a telescope has not been fully explored. This research demonstrates that astronomical photometry can effectively measure atmospheric optical depth around a telescope, utilizing images of stars taken during routine broad-spectrum observations to assess light loss before it reaches the telescope. By employing a simple model to analyze these stellar light curves, the research derives atmospheric optical depth from the observed data. A dataset comprising 1160000000 stellar photometry readings collected over two years by the ROTSE-III burst detector is analyzed, revealing that atmospheric conditions near the telescope generally exhibit low levels of light scattering, with a median total optical depth of 0.056 across 103400000 observations occurring outside the city of Mendoza. In contrast, the data also identifies an increase in aerosol activity within the city, particularly under calm wind conditions, with a median optical depth of 0.078 observed inside Mendoza among 13100000 readings, and allows for real-time aerosol monitoring using existing burst detector systems.

Numerous algorithms have been developed over the years to explore the complex free energy landscapes of molecular systems, particularly in statistical physics simulations known as Molecular Dynamics (MD). While a highly effective code called SMOLDYN was created many years ago for these purposes, an improved version named OLDYN has been developed and presents several significant advancements. OLDYN seamlessly integrates external and internal forces, supports time-varying temperature conditions, and utilizes an exact solver for harmonic oscillators along with a higher-order integrator for non-linear configurations, reducing energy dissipation during simulations. Furthermore, OLDYN is highly scalable and can efficiently handle large molecular systems with thousands of particles. Extensive tests have been conducted to evaluate its performance, comparing it with other MD codes and demonstrating its superior accuracy and efficiency. OLDYN has been found to accurately model the Brownian motion of a Brownian particle and the equilibrium state of a Lennard-Jones ring, and simulations of a Sharpe function-minimizing trimer of Lennard-Jones particles show results nearly identical to NPT ensemble Monte Carlo measurements. Overall, the updated and configurable OLDYN code offers precise and efficient configurational molecular sampling under various pressure and temperature conditions, making it a valuable and open-source tool available at GitHub.

Human evaluation metrics like accuracy and F1 scores are commonly used to assess image description generation models. Although widely adopted, it has been discovered that these evaluation measures are heavily influenced by biases inherent in the human data used to create them. This bias manifests itself in models' outputs, skewing evaluation results. To investigate this issue, researchers examined the AIS托 dataset, finding an unusually high accuracy rate of over 80% for non-descriptive sentences in the validation set. This characteristic, along with its suitability for machine translation, makes it highly susceptible to manipulation by models, rendering it unsuitable for reliably evaluating image description generators. A more appropriate alternative, text-to-video models, are suggested for evaluating generated descriptions. Additionally, the study examined the prevalence of copy-paste bias in these models. Overall, the research highlights the inadequacy of current evaluation practices, calling for the development of better, unbiased evaluation methods.

We integrate intricate aspects of conformal field theory (CFT) complexity with intrinsic mathematical dynamics in Euler-Arnold equation models to produce a intricate roadmap for determining central charges and field theory intricacy measures such as the max entropy central charge and the complexizing parameter. Specifically, we establish that the complexizing parameter corresponds to the CT invariant $\nu$ and demonstrate that its viable values align precisely with theoretically acceptable central charge values in CFT models. Furthermore, we establish that optimal entropy central charge values in the CFT framework correspond exactly to invariant functional values in the Euler-Arnold context and, consequently, are restricted to specific functional values.

This work extends a multiple input multiple output (MISO) - OFDM optimization model developed previously, addressing new scenarios with single antenna and or multiple antennas under a specific fade-out time limit. Additionally, of the various optimization models, revised versions are created that incorporate a minimum required data rate constraint and explore alternative optimization strategies. In the expanded MISO - OFDM model, the constraint is applied to each carrier individually, whereas in the SISO/OFDM and MISO/OFDM variants, the optimization process is restructured without directly imposing the constraint on the model itself.

We present a framework specifically for fitting probability density functions, with an emphasis on statistical inference. This model incorporates three key components: the data representation, the fitting process, and the use of likelihood ratios for decision making. The underlying statistical theory relies on composite hypothesis testing, with an emphasis on likelihood ratio principles. We illustrate the utility of this framework through various PDF fitting examples, both theoretical and practical. Furthermore, we propose three enhancements for improving PDF fitting outcomes: incorporating more informative error structures, utilizing multi-dimensional PDF fitting, and utilizing robust fitting methods to reduce the impact of outliers.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of an hydrocarbon jet flame's response to acoustic fluctuations to recreate flame instability patterns observed in previous studies. To facilitate this investigation, a computational model was developed that incorporates real-world measurements of turbulent jet flame dynamics, utilizing an active flame approach where the flame's dynamics are simulated through chemical solvers integrated within a CFD code (Fire). Acoustic fluctuations were incorporated into the code through a solver for linearized Navier-Stokes equations (Nek5000), with an initial state derived from the CFD code and a time-evolving solution resulting from the LS method. To better understand the sources of oscillating flame behavior, the model's results were analyzed, focusing on resonance patterns and instability ranges observed in previous experiments. A map was created that correlates resonance frequencies with jet velocity and nozzle diameter, revealing a more complex relationship between these variables and frequency than previously understood. Additionally, an investigation was conducted on the relationship between flame oscillation intensity and jet velocity, revealing a non-linear pattern that mirrors experimental observations. Overall, the study's findings provide a foundation for predicting flame instability patterns in jet flames and enable the exploration of flame response to acoustic fluctuations in a computational framework. A further investigation is suggested to validate the model's results through experimental data.

Nonlocal gravity theory posits that the relationship between the metric tensor and the gravitational stress-energy tensor involves integrals over past events. This type of theory is ideal for exploring innovative nonlocal models. A nonlocal version of Teichmann-Scheiderer gravity is described, which is applicable when both the gravitational potential and shape of spacetime are taken into account. In this particular model, the curvature tensor is related to the Ricci-squared term in a nonlocal manner. This allows the graph of spacetime geometry to be derived from the (nonlocal) gravitational potential. A similar nonlocal framework is presented where the gravitational potential is defined as the variant of the higher-order tensor, unambiguous within the context of metric theory. This enables the determination of gravitational potential in terms of (nonlocal) curvature. These constitutive relations are applicable when evaluating three-dimensional models of gravity. A nonlocal, variational approach is described, which allows the derivation of nonlocal gravity models in which metric, and gravitational potential are treated as independent fields. This leads to a nonlocal version of general relativity where both fields are incorporated into the model. A local version of this framework is described, which is applicable when the metric tensor is derived from the gravitational potential in a local context. This results in a nonlocal variant of the Einstein-ArkHamiltonian field equations, in which the metric tensor and gravitational potential are taken into account. This paper provides an in-depth summary of the conditions required for various
exotic physics processes involving only heavy-ion collisions, both alone and in
combination with proton collisions, and explores their potential for discovering
new physics, particularly in the context of ultra-peripheral collisions, within
the LHCC master schedule. Unlike processes such as charmonium production or
muon pair generation, which are frequently discussed, this report delves into
the specific requirements for observing diverse physics phenomena at both ion
colliders and (uncommonly) proton colliders, showcasing the potential richness
of heavy-ion and mixed collision experiments.

Observations of some nearby pulsars showing rapid magnetic field decay suggest that neutron star magnetic fields may not be highly uniform right after formation. We propose that strong magnetic fields might not be a necessary characteristic of X-ray binary pulsars. We develop a recurrence formula for magnetar bursts in X-ray binary systems, taking into account the distribution of neutron stars and normal stars in the galaxy along with various magnetic field decay rates. This formula closely mirrors previous estimates of such events but may actually show greater variability. We also discuss possible characteristics of neutron star X-ray binary transient events, noting that the magnetic field decay rate and initial strength of the neutron star could affect the recurrence interval of such events. Varying the initial magnetic field strength of the neutron star in our recurrence formula results in intervals that match those seen in observations when a moderate reduction in magnetic field straight after birth is assumed. We further discuss possible effects of the magnetic field strength of the star and the mass of its binary companion on the recurrence interval of such events. We also consider possible roles played by neutron star spin-up events and gas disk conditions in the Milky Way in these events. Additionally, we examine the properties of ten close, low-mass X-ray binary systems with long residence times in the Galactic Centre region, suggesting that the star with the strongest initial magnetic field in this area may in fact be a pulsar. We predict that such systems should exhibit low X-ray emission rates and relatively fast X-ray variability. Future astrophysical observations could help

Bipartite graphs that represent connections between distinct groups of objects are widely used in various fields. To enhance their utility, new edges can be added by combining parts of the groups, a process known as vertex splitting. Unfortunately, this information about merged entities is often lost during such splittings. To overcome this challenge, an efficient algorithmic approach called vertex recovery has been developed. While finding the optimal vertex recovery plan is computationally intensive for large graphs, a powerful algorithm has been created that guarantees minimal changes to the graph and limits vertex merging within groups to at most a specified number $r$, in polynomial time relative to the number of vertices. Additionally, it's been established that if the initial graph satisfies a specific condition involving the size of one group and a parameter $\omega(-,G)$, optimal vertex recovery plans will also meet this requirement.

This study presents a novel GPGPU voltage and frequency acceleration method that overcomes limitations imposed by conventional optimization techniques. While gradual optimization methods like SGX and DXE offer significant improvements (e.g., 30% and 60% respectively), they often result in substantial data corruption (up to 99.99% and 80% respectively). Our proposed method, HyperDegrade, achieves an impressive 80% and 60% speedup for voltage and frequency adjustments respectively, with negligible corruption levels (less than 0.1% and 1% respectively). Furthermore, HyperDegrade enables aggressive frequency reductions (e.g., from 2.1GHz to 400MHz) that are unattainable through conventional methods. We believe this research has significant implications for various applications including energy exploration, security research, and performance analysis.

A non-trivial disentangling maneuver for classical and welded links is proposed during a study on link theory. This Disintegrate operator, which is defined as a dual to the closure operator mentioned in the Burnside theorem, is demonstrated to be effective in disproving two longstanding conjectures associated with classical wounds links and autocatalytic links within the welded braid monoid. By Disintegrate closure being identified as a generalized Maragoto operator, it is established that the proposed Disintegrate operator enables the disintegration of specific intricate linked structures. Moreover, its reliability is verified through practical implementation.

Synchronization techniques have been implemented in a wide variety of applications including consensus, sampling, coordination, and consensus-based decision making. Most existing research assumes synchronization occurs when tasks share a common feature such as name, type, or purpose. This paper diverges from this norm by focusing on time-based synchronization that considers tasks with distinct names but identical types occurring at different times. A strategic synchronization policy is derived that maximizes the total number of executed tasks over a specified period through optimal determination of synchronization moments. The optimal solution is proven to consist of clustering tasks by rank and executing them in groups. A stochastic synchronization policy is also examined and found to result in a power-law distribution of task execution times.

This study aims to establish that both general linear groups $G_n(\mathbb{C})$ and special orthogonal groups $O_n(\mathbb{C})$ can be embedded into the wreath product $U_{2^{n-2}}(\mathbb{C}) \wr S_4$ and $U_{2^{n-1}}(\mathbb{C}) \wr S_2$, respectively. Previously, we proved in 2022 that these general linear and orthogonal groups could be embedded into the power of $U_m(\mathbb{C})$ where $m=2^{n-2}$ and $2^{n-1}$ respectively, and we demonstrated that these groups could also be embedded into $4\times4$ block matrices. However, the current paper presents a more efficient method by embedding these groups into the $4\times4$ block matrices within the wreath product structure, thereby improving the dimension of the constituent matrices in the matrix multiplication model. The required dimension of the matrix components in this new representation is $2^{(n-2)\times2}$ and $2^{(n-1)\times2}$ for $G_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $O_n(\mathbb{C})$ respectively, compared to the prior requirement of $2^{n-2}$ and $2^{n-1}$ respectively.
